Description

Osteopontin, a phosphorylated matrix protein of bone, rises in the synovial fluid and plasma of patients with knee osteoarthritis, and its levels follow radiographic severity. Several tissues of the osteoarthritic joint make it: osteoblasts of the sclerotic subchondral bone, chondrocytes of degenerating cartilage, in step with the severity of the lesions, and synoviocytes, which also respond to it through CD44 and integrin αvβ3. Mast cells, activated in osteoarthritic joints through IgE and its receptor FcεRI, make osteopontin too. Osteopontin binds CD44 and integrin αv on mast cells and strengthens their IgE-triggered degranulation and migration. Degranulation releases histamine, which sensitises nociceptors through the H1 receptor. A direct action of osteopontin on nociceptors has not been shown.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Metabolites take a lighter shade of the same colour. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Osteopontin, IgE and their receptors are red: they activate mast cells, which release histamine and other mediators of pain and inflammation.
